cells.tense: You are keeping fair exchange alive and moving here, right now, with your own hand on it.
cells.ask: Give one fair pattern your circle already runs — who brings what to a gathering, how a song gets credited — a shape it can keep without your hand on it.
cells.core:
You keep exchange fair here. When something gets shared — a role, a story, a turn — people end up with as much as they put in. That's rare in a group with a memory. It holds because you treat it as a practice, not a mood.

One fair pattern your circle already runs could outlast your presence in it. Put that pattern into a form that doesn't lean on you — written into how the next gathering is run, taught to someone who'll carry it, built into the rhythm of the thing itself. Then fairness has a shape of its own. It holds on the days you aren't there to hold it.

cells.tense: You are bracing for a fair exchange that has not happened yet, running the books ahead of the room.
cells.act: carry your own share, all of it
cells.ask: For one week, bring exactly your own portion to the shared thing — your dish, your notes, your part — and stop tracking what anybody else gives.
cells.core:
You are running the accounts ahead of time. Who gave what, who still owes, what's fair before anyone has spoken — the ledger runs in the back while you're supposed to be part of the thing. Keeping it even has become the work. But balance held that tightly stops being balance. It becomes a scale the others can feel on them, and the gathering shrinks.

For one week, carry your full share and nothing beyond it. Let the meal itself hold your attention, nothing else. If a share goes missing, you'll see it at week's end. Fairness done this way gets its rhythm back. You bring, they bring, the table fills.

cells.tense: You stopped bringing anything to the shared table a while back, and you are still standing near it.
cells.act: strike one thing from the list that does not serve
cells.ask: Go through what you do for the group and cross off a single habit of showing up. Don't hand anything else out. Before the next gathering, notice which of the remaining habits still fits the room.
cells.core:
You're close to the shared thing, and you've gone quiet in it. What you contribute has stopped arriving — the stories, the corrections, the parts you used to show up with. You watch. You're good at reading a room. But reading has replaced joining, and the exchange inside you runs on one side.

Before you try to give more, sharpen what you're already carrying. Take what you do for the group and strike off something you only do because it has long been done. Just the striking, not an announcement. What's left gets clearer. Refinement like this isn't withdrawal — it's how a practice stays honest. The room still wants you in it.

cells.tense: You are already keeping this group fair, and you'd say the group simply has a good way of doing things.
cells.act: hold two true things without declaring either
cells.ask: Some quiet moment this week, bring to mind a swap you evened out on purpose — a turn handed back, a gap covered — and see it as something you chose. Say it to no one.
cells.core:
In this shared thing, somebody keeps the exchange fair — covers a gap, hands back a turn, says the thing that puts credit where it's owed. That somebody reads how a group's scales work. Asked about any of it, you'd say the group just has a good way. It does. It also has a hand in it.

When you're about to even something up, pause before you move. Stay a breath with it, seeing that this is yours to do, then do it or leave it. The deed is the same either way. What shifts is whether you know your part in it. The act stays yours when you see it as yours.
cells.sheetLine: The fairness here is yours. You file it under how things are done.
